text: This lesson covers JSON, the plain-text format that structured data travels in between systems, and the two built-in methods that move data in and out of that format on the server side.

A JSON string looks like a JavaScript object, but it's just plain text until you parse it - you can't read a property off it directly, the way you would off a real object. JSON.parse takes that string and converts it into a real object with actual properties you can reference, which is exactly what a Scripted REST API resource has to do with an inbound request body before it can use any of the data the calling system sent.

JSON.stringify does the reverse: it takes a real JavaScript object and turns it into a JSON-formatted string, ready to log, send in a response body, or pass somewhere that only accepts plain text. This is the exact mechanism a Scripted REST API uses to send structured data back to whoever called it, something you'll build in depth in a later course on IntegrationHub and REST APIs.

Put together, a realistic flow looks like this: parse the incoming request body into an object, read values like caller and priority off it, and build a GlideRecord from those values. If you need to respond with data instead, you'd build a plain object describing the result and stringify it on the way out.

Parse and stringify are inverses of each other - stringifying an object and then parsing that string back gives you an equivalent object, with the same properties and values intact. That round-trip property is what makes JSON a safe way to pass structured data through anything that only accepts plain text, like a GlideAjax parameter, a scratchpad value, or a log entry.
Next is the Server-Side JavaScript Lab, where scope, string and date handling, and JSON all come together in one real worked scenario, built as a single reusable Script Include method.
